opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I'd frame it is that most of the industry started from training and worked backward to inference. The big GPU platforms were built to train massive models, and rack-scale for them means building an enormous, tightly coupled supercomputer, with very expensive interconnect and a lot of power and liquid cooling, so thousands of chips can act like one giant processor for weeks-long training runs. That's an engineering feat, but it isn't necessarily what inference needs.

We started from the opposite end. From day one d-Matrix has been an inference company. What matters in inference is memory bandwidth and latency. The bottleneck isn't raw compute. It's how quickly you can move model weights and the KV cache to where the math happens. So we built our compute around memory, with digital in-memory compute and a chiplet-based design, so data barely has to travel.

That philosophy carries into the rack. We don't think you have to rebuild the whole data center to serve models efficiently. Our approach is to fit into the infrastructure customers already have: standard form factors, standard Ethernet-based networking, air-cooled where possible, and working with partners across the ecosystem instead of forcing a fully proprietary stack. When we scale out across cards and servers, we focus on keeping latency low as tokens move between devices, because in inference that hop-to-hop latency shows up directly in the user experience.

So the distinction is this: others offer a training architecture that also does inference, and that comes with a training-sized cost and power bill. We offer a rack designed around the economics of inference: tokens per second per watt, tokens per dollar, and very fast interactive response. As AI moves into reasoning models, agents, and long-context workloads, inference becomes the dominant workload. We think the rack should be built for that reality, not retrofitted to it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions scaling across cards and servers, but does not say d-Matrix sells cards or trays while competitors sell complete racks.

r002.rationale: It mentions working with ecosystem partners, but does not state that partners sell complete racks containing d-Matrix hardware.

r003.rationale: It does not mention hyperscalers building their own racks or connect that to d-Matrix not needing to sell complete racks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to understand is that we didn't start with the chip and then work our way up to the rack. We started with the workload, which for us is inference, and we asked what the rack needs to look like if inference is the only thing it ever does. And then we designed backward from that.

Most of the industry is still carrying a legacy that came from training. You have these big, power-hungry accelerators, HBM stacked around them, and then you spend an enormous amount of effort on the interconnect to make hundreds or thousands of them behave like one giant machine. That's the right answer for training. It's a very expensive answer for inference, because inference is fundamentally a memory-bandwidth problem, not a flops problem. You're moving weights and KV cache around constantly, and the compute sits idle waiting on memory.

So our approach with Corsair is digital in-memory compute. We put the compute right next to the SRAM, so the data doesn't have to travel across a package or out to HBM every time. That changes the economics of the whole rack. Each card is lower power, we don't need exotic cooling, and we can fit in a standard air-cooled enclosure that a normal data center already knows how to run. We're not asking customers to rip out their infrastructure and build a liquid-cooled pod.

The second difference is how we scale. We treat the rack as the unit of deployment, but we scale out across cards with a fairly conventional fabric rather than trying to make the rack look like one monolithic chip. For inference, you don't need every accelerator talking to every other one at full speed. You need to map a model across a handful of cards efficiently, serve a lot of users concurrently, and keep latency per token low and predictable. That's a very different design center from the all-to-all problem in training.

And honestly, the third thing is just the business model. We're not trying to be the one chip for everything. We're saying the market is going to bifurcate. Training will stay with a small number of very large players and very large systems. Inference is going to be everywhere, at much higher volume, and the cost per token is what wins. If you optimize the entire rack for that one metric, you end up in a very different place than the companies that are adapting training hardware to run inference.

r001.rationale: The response says the rack is d-Matrix’s unit of deployment and describes scaling across cards, but it does not distinguish its card-or-tray unit of sale from competitors’ rack-level unit of sale.

r002.rationale: It does not identify external partners as responsible for selling complete racks that include d-Matrix hardware.

r003.rationale: It does not say that hyperscalers build their own racks or that this removes any need for d-Matrix to sell complete racks.

astra-6.text:
The way I’d distinguish our approach is that we start with inference as a system problem. It’s not enough to build a fast chip and then assume that putting a lot of those chips in a rack gives you an efficient inference platform. You have to think about how the model is distributed, how data moves between chips, and what that means for latency, throughput, and power.

With d-Matrix, digital in-memory computing is the foundation, and we design the interconnect and software around it. The objective is to carry that efficiency through to the rack, so customers get useful inference capacity at an attractive cost. That’s the distinction: we’re designing toward the performance of the complete system, rather than treating rack-scale deployment as something that comes after the chip.

sol-6.1.text:
The way we think about rack-scale deployment is to start with the inference workload and design the system around it. It’s not just about putting a fast chip on a board and then putting a lot of boards in a rack. You have to think about how the compute, memory, and interconnect work together, because moving data can become the bottleneck.

With d-Matrix, our approach is built around digital in-memory computing, bringing computation closer to where the data resides. Then we carry that thinking through the system: how do you connect the devices, distribute the workload, and keep them busy while meeting the latency requirements of inference?

So the distinction is really the unit of optimization. We’re looking at the performance and economics of the whole inference system—latency, throughput, power, and cost—rather than treating the rack as simply a collection of individually optimized chips.
